This page covers the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC occupation 47-4051.00, Highway Maintenance Workers: maintaining highways, municipal and rural roads, airport runways, and rights-of-way. Duties include patching broken or eroded pavement and repairing guardrails, highway markers, and snow fences; workers may also mow or clear brush along roads or plow snow from roadways. Official scope: Maintain highways, municipal and rural roads, airport runways, and rights-of-way. Duties include patching broken or eroded pavement and repairing guard rails, highway markers, and snow fences. May also mow or clear brush from along road, or plow snow from roadway. O*NET lists the following core tasks (19 tasks are listed, with the first 5 displayed by default): placing signs and cones around work areas to divert traffic; flagging motorists or warning them of obstacles or repairs ahead; performing preventive maintenance on vehicles and heavy equipment; driving trucks to transport crews and equipment to worksites; and using hand and power tools to erect, install, or repair guardrails, shoulders, slope protection, highway signs, warning signals, and highway lighting. Common job titles include Highway Maintenance Worker, Highway Maintainer, Highway Maintenance Technician, Equipment Operator, and Transportation Maintenance Operator. Coverage note: the U.S. wage and employment data on O*NET's 47-4051.00 page are not identified as coming from a broader or adjacent occupation; this page accurately labels them as data for this occupation itself (47-4051.00). In the U.S., it is in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0). This page does not extrapolate U.S. coverage to job titles, qualifications, or wages in mainland China.

Practice brief | A wholly fictional highway maintenance task package, solely for practicing the process and representing no real road section, organization, or data. Draft a plan covering: (1) how to use a fictional maintenance work order and road-section information to structure pavement patching or ancillary-facility maintenance: section, chainage, and lane; defect type and repair method; materials, tools, and equipment; work-zone layout, signs, cones, and flaggers; traffic diversion and traffic-police coordination; weather, visibility, and timing; and cleanup and reopening to traffic. Specify missing information to obtain: road structure and traffic volume; site, underground utilities, and slope conditions; safety, access, and work-permit requirements; material delivery; and coordination with the maintenance schedule. (2) How to design completion and review points for a fictional maintenance and work record: fields and definitions, section and work-order identifiers, materials and quantities, work-zone layout and traffic management, repairs and quality, exceptions, rework and outstanding items, and original records and revision trails. (3) How to write a handover-ready shift and work summary: section and chainage—defects and method—materials and quantities—traffic management—post-work condition—outstanding items and recommendations. (4) How to record and retain maintenance and work data, distinguishing public information from controlled organization and road-section materials. (5) How to pause, reassess, isolate, and report upon discovering traffic conflicts, sudden weather changes, machinery or fall risks, matters beyond the role's authority, or safety risks. Use public materials and simulated data, never real road-section or organization data.

Responsibility check | Actual fit depends on accomplishing three things within the same operation: doing the technical work properly—following procedures and work orders to set up work zones, maintain roads, clean up, and keep usable maintenance and work records; controlling safety, compliance, and boundaries—working and keeping records according to requirements for work-zone layout, signs, cones, flaggers, traffic diversion, personal protection, and weather, distinguishing public information from controlled organization and road-section materials and handling them under policy, and never closing lanes or acting beyond authority without authorization; and accepting defined job responsibilities—being accountable for your own work-zone setup, maintenance, cleanup, and records, while referring matters beyond your authority or involving traffic control or major safety issues to the appropriate role or organization under policy. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as preparing an assisted-work plan and an explanation of maintenance and work records for a fictional work order, or reviewing a response to a traffic conflict, sudden weather change, or machinery abnormality, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

(ii) Pavement and ancillary-structure maintenance—patching broken or eroded pavement and erecting, installing, or repairing guardrails, shoulders, slope protection, highway signs, warning signals, and highway lighting. entries.answer: Highway Maintenance Workers on this page is the exact O*NET occupation 47-4051.00, Highway Maintenance Workers: maintaining highways, municipal and rural roads, airport runways, and rights-of-way. Duties include patching broken or eroded pavement and repairing guardrails, highway markers, and snow fences; workers may also mow or clear brush along roads or plow snow from roadways. The page lists 19 tasks. The most important include placing signs and cones around work areas to divert traffic, flagging motorists or warning them of obstacles or repairs ahead, preventive maintenance on vehicles and heavy equipment, driving trucks to transport crews and equipment to worksites, and using hand and power tools to erect, install, or repair guardrails, shoulders, slope protection, highway signs, warning signals, and highway lighting. Common titles include Highway Maintenance Worker, Highway Maintainer, and Equipment Operator.

subject.name: Highway Maintenance Workers
subject.summary: Highway Maintenance Workers corresponds to the exact O*NET/SOC occupation 47-4051.00, Highway Maintenance Workers: maintaining highways, municipal and rural roads, airport runways, and rights-of-way. Duties include patching broken or eroded pavement and repairing guardrails, highway markers, and snow fences; workers may also mow or clear brush along roads or plow snow from roadways. Core tasks include placing signs and cones around work areas to divert traffic; flagging motorists or warning them of obstacles or repairs ahead; performing preventive maintenance on vehicles and heavy equipment; driving trucks to transport crews and equipment to worksites; and using hand and power tools to erect, install, or repair guardrails, shoulders, slope protection, highway signs, warning signals, and highway lighting. Common job titles include Highway Maintenance Worker, Highway Maintainer, Highway Maintenance Technician, and Equipment Operator. Official scope: Maintain highways, municipal and rural roads, airport runways, and rights-of-way. Duties include patching broken or eroded pavement and repairing guard rails, highway markers, and snow fences. May also mow or clear brush from along road, or plow snow from roadway. Coverage note: the U.S. wage, employment, and industry data presented on O*NET's 47-4051.00 page are not identified as coming from a broader or adjacent occupation; this page accurately labels them as data for this occupation itself (47-4051.00). The occupation is in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0), with Average growth (3% to 4%) for 2024–2034. This page does not constitute safety, traffic, special operations, occupational health, or legal advice.
